newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - British ad agency finds new ways to work.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - British ad agency finds new ways to work.

text.p: Advertising agencies are known for using off-beat methods to stimulate staff creativity -- but few go so far as to deck out offices like a teenager's bedroom or allow employees to vote for their own pay rises.
But British-based St Luke's, which claims to be the world's only advertising agency run as a cooperative, says it is proud of taking things to the limit.

Employees have no individual desks or offices, but there is a room painted red and called "the womb" for quiet work, and staff are encouraged to get inspiration from themed rooms, including one that looks like a train carriage.
The agency says potential clients are flocking to see its unorthodox ways of working.
"We are getting so many major companies and management gurus coming in to see how we work that we are having to set up organised tours once a month," says marketing director David Abraham.

St Luke's -- named after the patron saint of artists -- was formed when Abraham and Andy Law led a management buyout in October 1995 of the London office of Chiat Day, a U.S.-based agency belonging to Omnicom Group Inc .
Law, a founding director of Chiat Day, is now chairman of St Luke's.

"We wanted to do something radical. Many ad agencies have a very hierarchical structure and exist only to benefit shareholders you never meet or owners with little direct involvement, so we created a corporate structure to match our ideals," Abraham told Reuters.
EQUAL SHARES
Everyone in St Luke's, from the receptionist to the managing director, gets an equal number of shares in the agency.

"The deal with Omnicom meant that they left an element of working capital in St Luke's. Omnicom will get a percentage of our income, which is a combination of client fees and profits. The percentage rises as our income rises. For our first million they get two percent, from the next (million), four percent and so on over seven years," says finance director Neil Thompson.

All staff have the opportunity to vote on the size of their next pay rise. Although salaries differ, they differ less than in many other agencies. And performance reviews are done not only by bosses about subordinates, but by staff about their managers.
Employees vote on virtually every aspect of their working lives, from the colour of the walls to the agency's future direction.
"This summer the staff elected to slow down on the new business front and to concentrate on and enjoy what we already have. We are calling it the 'summer of love'," said Abraham.
But he says St Luke's is a serious agency and not some sort of "hippy" organisation.
St Luke's now handles advertising business worth more than 40 million pounds ($67.1 million).
It has attracted a string of clients including Midland Bank, Boots the Chemist Plc, United Distillers and furniture retailer Ikea.
"We are a 'top 30 agency' now and we will not pitch for accounts worth less than five million pounds," said Abraham.
THEMED ROOMS FOR INSPIRATION
As well as having an unusual management structure the agency also looks like no other.

It is housed in a converted toffee factory and has an artist in residence who has created wild sculptures around the building. Staff have only lockers for their personal belongings and each person carries a mobile phone at all times. Computer terminals are scattered around the building and staff can choose to work in "the womb", the "chill out" room, or even the coffee room if they wish.
An in-house masseur is available to all staff and the creative director's father, a former chef, prepares an Italian lunch every day.
But perhaps the most unusual aspect of the agency is that each client has its own themed room to act as a source of inspiration.

St Luke's works on the Boots Number 17 cosmetics account, a brand that is aimed at teenage girls, and the Boots room is decorated with pink walls, a bunk bed with pink duvets and posters of pop stars.

Eurostar, the Channel Tunnel rail company, has a room decorated to look like a train carriage complete with train seats, while the Clarks Shoes room contains a mini shoe shop. ($ = 0.596 British Pounds)
